title: Bank of Japan’s hawkish pause to leave scope for December hike
full_text:
Why look at real assets into 2027?
By Leika Kihara
TOKYO, Oct 26 (Reuters) - The Bank of Japan will likely declare victory in a nearly 14-year battle to hit its 2% inflation target at its policy meeting on Friday and emphasise the risks prices could overshoot, signaling the chance of a rate hike as soon as December.
Such hawkish language may reinforce expectations the BOJ, US Federal Reserve and European Central Bank will all raise rates by year-end, as brisk AI demand and the Iran war-induced energy shock worsen global inflationary pressures.
Still, the BOJ is likely to avoid dropping explicit hints on the timing and pace of future rate rises as it balances the need to forestall risks of an inflation overshoot without disrupting jittery markets with a premature hike, analysts say.
"With rises in prices and wages moderate, the BOJ will keep raising rates gradually without rushing," said a person familiar with its thinking, a view echoed by two more people.
At the two-day policy meeting ending on Friday, the BOJ is set to maintain its policy rate at 1.25% by a majority vote, forgoing a back-to-back hike to spend more time scrutinising the effect of past rate hikes on lending conditions.
In a quarterly report due after the meeting, the BOJ is likely to slightly revise up next fiscal year’s price forecast and signal that underlying inflation has roughly achieved its 2% target, people familiar with the matter have told Reuters.
With wage gains becoming embedded and inflation expectations hovering around 2%, the central bank will likely stress that it will now focus on anchoring inflation around its target by raising rates toward levels deemed neutral to the economy.
While Governor Kazuo Ueda has already signaled such a shift in policy focus upon raising rates in September, the pivot would mark another symbolic departure from the BOJ’s prolonged efforts to fire up inflation through ultra-loose monetary policy.
"It’s a historical moment for the BOJ, though it faces a more challenging task now that it needs to step not just on the accelerator but the brakes," said Naomi Muguruma, chief bond strategist at Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley Securities.
"The BOJ will probably scrutinise upcoming data and market moves in deciding whether to raise rates in December, or hold until January," she said.
Analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise rates to 1.5% in December and stick to a quarterly pace of rate hikes.
FUNDING STILL LOOSE
Under former governor Haruhiko Kuroda, the BOJ deployed a massive stimulus in 2013 to pull Japan out of deflation and fire up inflation to its 2% inflation target.
Even after ending its mix of unorthodox easing steps in 2024, the central bank has trodden cautiously in raising rates on the view underlying inflation - or price moves excluding one-off factors and driven by domestic demand - remained below target.
With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised rates in September after delivering a hike in June - a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes in 2024 and 2025.
The BOJ’s policy rate, at 1.25%, is now within the range of 1.1% to 2.5% its staff estimated as Japan’s neutral rate, or the level that neither cools nor overheats the economy - drawing market attention to how far it could eventually hike rates.
With growth in bank lending still strong, the central bank is likely to stress on Friday that financial conditions remain loose - signalling scope for further rate hikes before its policy rate reaches levels close to neutral, the people said.
The BOJ’s meeting follows that of the Fed, which is seen skipping a hike at its two-day meeting concluding on Wednesday. The ECB is also set to keep rates unchanged at 2.5% on Thursday.

SHANGHAI, Oct 26 (Reuters) - China’s yuan climbed to a fresh four-year high against the dollar on Monday, extending its longest winning streak since May, as softer oil prices and US Treasury yields weighed on the greenback, ahead of key policy meetings at home and overseas.
Investors were cautious ahead of major central bank meetings due later this week, with the US Federal Reserve, Bank of Japan and European Central Bank widely expected to keep rates unchanged while maintaining a hawkish tone. Attention will also turn to China’s fifth plenum for fresh policy clues.
Prior to market opening, the People’s Bank of China set the midpoint rate at 6.7162 per dollar, its strongest since February 2, 2023. The spot yuan is allowed to trade a maximum of 2% either side of the fixed midpoint each day.
Monday’s midpoint was 471 pips weaker than a Reuters estimate of 6.6691 — its largest weak-side deviation since September 23.
The central bank has been gradually strengthening its daily yuan official guidance this year, but at levels weaker than market expectations, suggesting it is seeking to manage the pace of appreciation, traders and analysts said.
"The PBOC continues to resist a faster pace of appreciation via weaker than-market-expected fixings," analysts at Barclays said in a note.
"We think the PBOC’s reaction function points to a stronger floor against disorderly weakness, while the fixing should continue to constrain the pace of gains as the trade-weighted currency strengthens."
In the spot market, the onshore yuan hit a high of 6.6682 per dollar at one point, the strongest level since June 2022, before last trading at 6.6691 as of 0252 GMT.
If it retains the gains at the late-night close, the onshore spot yuan would have booked an eighth straight session of rises, the longest winning streak since May.
Its offshore counterpart last fetched 6.6688 per dollar, up about 0.01% in Asian trade.
"We continue to think that a gradual but sustained currency appreciation is underway but consensus forecasts and forward markets underestimate how far this process can run given the deep undervaluation starting point," Goldman Sachs analysts said in a note.
"Ultimately, currency appreciation alone will not address China’s economic challenges ... that needs both currency appreciation and support for domestic demand, two instruments to hit two targets," they said, maintaining their 12-month target for the yuan at 6.40 per dollar.

title: GSK cancer drug clears rectal tumours in 76% of patients in trial, data shows
full_text:

Investing.com -- GSK Plc (LON:GSK) said on Monday its immunotherapy Jemperli cleared tumours completely in 76% of patients with a certain type of locally advanced rectal cancer, data that could let some patients skip chemotherapy, radiation and surgery.
The result comes from an exploratory analysis of AZUR-1, a phase II trial of Jemperli given on its own to adults with stage II and III rectal cancer with a genetic trait, MSI-H/dMMR, that stops tumours repairing DNA damage properly. In the analysis, 110 of 144 evaluable patients had a complete response.
That included 68% with a complete clinical response lasting at least 12 months without surgery, as assessed by investigators.
Another 12 had a complete response confirmed after surgery showed no cancer in tissue analysis. No recurrences have been reported among responders after median follow-up of more than two years.
AZUR-1 met its main goal of showing a clinically significant share of patients had a complete response lasting 12 months.
Judged by an independent central review, 47% of evaluable patients had reached that point at the time of analysis, with data still maturing. Another 38 had a complete response but had not yet reached 12 months.
Serious adverse reactions occurred in 20% of patients and 3% stopped treatment because of side effects.
Hesham Abdullah, GSK’s global head of oncology R&D, said: “For some patients, avoiding chemotherapy, radiation and surgery may now be possible.” The data supported the recent US approval of Jemperli for this use.
GSK separately reported results from BEHOLD-1, a phase I trial of its experimental antibody-drug conjugate mocertatug rezetecan (Mo-Rez), in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer.
At the dose chosen for phase III, Mo-Rez had a confirmed response rate of 62%, lasting a median 12.2 months; median progression-free survival, the time before disease worsened, was 11.1 months.
Grade 3 or higher treatment-related side effects, mostly blood-related, occurred in 71% of patients; 2% stopped treatment and 2% developed lung inflammation.
GSK, which acquired rights to Mo-Rez from Hansoh Pharma, has five pivotal phase III trials underway. Both datasets will be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology congress in Madrid.

Investing.com -- Sweden’s producer prices rose 3.4% in September from August, the biggest monthly increase since March 2022, lifting the annual rate to 11.2% from 6.8% as higher energy costs and a weaker crown fed through, Statistics Sweden said on Monday.
The annual rate was the highest since March 2023, said Carl Mårtensson, a price statistician at the agency.
Prices rose across all three markets in September from August, increasing 3.3% in the domestic market, 3.6% for exports and 4.5% for imports.
Annual rates were 10.2% for domestic sales, 12.4% for exports and 15.5% for imports, compared with 7%, 6.8% and 9.5%, respectively, in August.
Prices of energy-related products rose 42.1% from September 2025, while producer prices excluding energy increased 6.2% over the same period. Consumer goods prices rose 1% and capital goods prices 3.1% year on year.
In the domestic market, higher prices for electricity trading services contributed 1.9 percentage points to the monthly increase, while refined petroleum products added 1 percentage point.
Higher prices for basic chemicals, basic metals and district heating also contributed, partly offset by lower food prices.
Export prices were driven mainly by refined petroleum products, which added 1.2 percentage points, while electricity generation contributed 0.6 point. Import prices rose mainly due to crude oil, which added 2.5 percentage points, followed by refined petroleum products at 0.8 point.
The crown weakened against major trading currencies in September, pushing up export and import prices in crowns, the agency said.
Compared with August, the crown weakened 3% against the Norwegian krone, 2.6% against the dollar, 1.9% against the euro and Danish krone, and 1.6% against sterling.
Year on year, it weakened 9.4% against the Norwegian krone, 3.9% against the dollar and 2.1% against the euro.
The price index for domestic supply rose 3.9% in September from August and 12.9% year on year. The annual rate for consumer goods in the index rose to 0.6% in September from -0.1% in August.

title: Ready for a French test?: Five questions for the ECB
full_text:
Why look at real assets into 2027?
By Dhara Ranasinghe and Stefano Rebaudo
LONDON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - The European Central Bank meets on Thursday against a backdrop of upheaval in France and an Iran war that is keeping energy prices above $100, meaning inflation risks remain elevated.
"How do you set rates against that backdrop? It’s incredibly difficult," David Coombs, head of multi-asset investments at Rathbones Asset Management, said.
Here’s a look at five key questions for markets ahead of the October meeting.
1/ What will the ECB do?
Leave its key interest rate unchanged at 2.5%.
A pause is widely anticipated after the ECB raised rates in June and September to counter rising inflation, as the Iran war pushed up energy prices.
Economists polled by Reuters expect a quarter-point rate hike in December.
"I don’t think they’ve become materially less worried about inflation here," MUFG senior economist Henry Cook said.
2/ What will the ECB say about the rate outlook?
It’s likely to stick with a data-dependent approach.
Caught between high inflation, at 3.8% in September, and concerns that rising government bond yields could hurt growth, policymakers have recently argued for what ECB President Christine Lagarde called a "measured response."
"There will be a definite flag to the tightening in financial conditions and how it should slow growth and hence curb inflationary pressures," said Barclays’ head of euro rates strategy Rohan Khanna.
"But also, plenty of uncertainty around the conflict and the outlook for energy prices."
3/ How worried is the ECB about an energy-driven inflation rise?
Comments from officials such as ECB chief economist Philip Lane suggest the ECB is not overly worried, for now, about high energy costs leading to other prices and wages rising.
A muted increase in core inflation, which excludes food and fuel prices, to 2.5% last month from 2.4%, suggests that high energy costs have yet to generate the sort of second-round impacts that could set off a hard-to-break inflation spiral.
Still, with oil up 90% this year and headline inflation above its 2% target, the ECB will likely stress vigilance.
Euro zone consumers nudged up their inflation expectations for the next 12 months in September, a survey on Friday showed.
"If the war in Iran escalates, or if we see further pressure on energy prices, the risk is still more rate hikes in 2027," said Bas van Geffen, senior macro strategist at Rabobank, adding he did not have any penciled in for next year.
Markets price in at least two hikes by mid-2027.
4/ What about the French bond selloff?
Well, the ECB is watching.
French 10-year borrowing costs just hit 24-year highs above 5% and a weakened government is grappling with violent protests that could undermine efforts to improve fragile finances.
Also, the premium investors demand to hold 10-year French bonds over safer Germany is at 167 bps, up from 92 bps when the ECB met last month.
But don’t expect the ECB to act soon with measures such as the Transmission Protection Instrument that allows it to buy bonds from any member state experiencing an "unwarranted, disorderly" tightening of its financing conditions.
France should solve its own debt problems through fiscal consolidation, says Lagarde.
The ECB could hold back on rate hikes if it thinks a crisis in France could hurt economic growth materially, Berenberg chief economist Holger Schmieding said.
"If there are serious contagion effects from a hypothetical French crisis to other countries where the fiscal policy is much more sustainable, the ECB would probably use its TPI to shield these other countries, not France," he said.
5/ Who will replace Lagarde?
The ECB chief, who could be appointed as the next World Economic Forum chair as early as November, will likely be pressed on succession.
The former central bank governors of the Netherlands and Spain, Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, are seen as frontrunners.
Lagarde’s exit would open a second vacancy on the ECB’s six-member Executive Board after Isabel Schnabel’s recent resignation. Chief economist Lane will step down in May.
Lagarde’s term is scheduled to end next October. Leaving early allows time for a new ECB chief to be picked before France’s spring presidential election. A snap Spanish election could also impact the politics around ECB succession, analysts said.

title: Chinese beauty brands, flush with success at home, start to vie for global shelf space
full_text:
Why look at real assets into 2027?
By Casey Hall and Dominique Patton
SHANGHAI/PARIS, Oct 26 (Reuters) - China’s beauty brands are stepping out into the global market, armed with intricately carved lipsticks, freeze-dried face masks activated with purified water as well as creams infused with ingredients from traditional Chinese medicine.
Proya Cosmetics, the largest C-beauty brand by revenue, is among the most aggressive. Its Advanced Firming and Original Repair skincare lines will be sold in 400 Ulta stores as well as on Ulta.com across the United States from November, and it opened a Paris research and development centre this month.
Other brands had their start in online sales and are now expanding to physical stores abroad. They include Florasis, whose lipsticks and other ornate cosmetics draw on traditional Chinese aesthetics. It opened its first overseas flagship shop in Tokyo’s posh Ginza district last year.
Joocyee, which produces skincare-infused makeup, and Judydoll, known for inventive products such as its metal-wand mascara, opened shops in Singapore last year. Both brands, owned by China’s Joy Group, are also now stocked at Skin Cupid, a British retailer specialising in Asian beauty products.
C-beauty brands have grown rapidly within China over the past decade and industry executives today speak of a growing confidence that Chinese products will find favour with consumers worldwide. Gone are the days when China was associated with cheap and low-quality goods, as Chinese innovations — across many industries but particularly in electric vehicles — have produced a halo effect, they say.
"The shift can be seen in everything from cars and smartphones to AI models," said David Huang, CEO of New York-listed Yatsen Group, which owns the Perfect Diary makeup brand.
The efforts by the C-beauty firms are part of a broader push abroad by Chinese brands — from fashion and electronics to bubble tea — keen to seek new revenue amid a years-long slump in domestic consumer spending.
BRAND AWARENESS CHALLENGES AHEAD
Some Chinese brands are very ambitious. Proya, for example, wants to become a top 10 brand globally and is among C-beauty companies exploring acquisitions of smaller foreign brands to expand their portfolios.
Its 51%-owned colour cosmetics brand Flower Knows, known for fairytale-inspired packaging, also launched with British pharmacy and beauty retailer Boots in March and began a limited run in Ulta stores in September.
While awareness of Chinese beauty brands is growing in many international markets, Proya says it has a long way to go.
"I would say that Proya’s brand awareness in both Europe and the US is currently zero," founder and CEO Hou Juncheng said at the opening of the company’s R&D centre in Paris.
"We hope that through collaboration with our partners, we can earn consumer trust and encourage them to purchase our products."
Rivals believe Proya, founded only 20 years ago, has a bright future, with Marc-Antoine Jamet, president of French industry association Cosmetic Valley, describing Hou as an "incredible competitor".
"He moved from the mass market to the mid-market, and then from the mid-market to the premium segment. You can be sure he’ll move into the luxury sector — whether in six weeks, six months, or six years. That’s a near certainty," said Jamet.
CONQUERING AT HOME AND INSPIRED BY K-BEAUTY
C-beauty brands overtook international names in 2022 and accounted for 57.4% of China’s $159 billion cosmetics market last year, according to the China Association of Fragrance, Flavor and Cosmetic Industries.
They can also draw inspiration from the success of their Korean counterparts, which have become a significant force in the global cosmetics industry.
Exports for the K-beauty sector, known for 10-step routines to produce luminous "glass skin", surged 50% over five years to hit $11.4 billion in 2025. South Korea also overtook France in 2024 to become the top source of cosmetics imports in the tough-to-crack American market, US International Trade Commission data showed.
K-beauty has helped pave the way by bringing "this Asian cultural awareness to the market," said Jing An, an attorney at Altman & An, a New York law firm that helps foreign firms with US intellectual property and e-commerce operations.
An says her Chinese clients are usually apparel firms, luggage brands and online platforms but in the past year she has taken on two Chinese beauty clients looking to enter the US market.
One advantage that Chinese brands might have is their mid-market price points. Global consumers have become "really fed up of paying premium prices for topical skincare," said Elisa Harca, co-founder of marketing firm Red Ant Asia, which has advised global retailers on which C-beauty products to stock.
In the US, Chinese brands must also navigate persistent trade and geopolitical tensions between Beijing and Washington. Gabby Chen, president of global markets at Florasis, said that last year, China-US tensions led the brand to shift its international expansion away from the US.
Chen is more optimistic today, saying her focus is on building a sustainable, long-term global business regardless of the geopolitical backdrop. People who choose to buy Florasis are likely to be more international and open-minded, she added.
"It doesn’t have to be political. It’s like Feng Shui, you can choose to believe it or not, but we are here to share with you the essence of our culture and the essence of our brand."

title: Genmab shares jump 13% on colorectal cancer drug trial results
full_text:

Investing.com -- Genmab shares jumped as much as 13% on Monday after the Danish biotech said its experimental drug petosemtamab, combined with chemotherapy, shrank tumours in 75% of previously untreated patients with advanced colorectal cancer in a mid-stage trial.
The 75% figure combines confirmed and unconfirmed responses among first-line patients who could be evaluated, after a median follow-up of 5.9 months. In second-line patients, treated after one earlier chemotherapy regimen, the rate was 67% after a median follow-up of 7.1 months.
With longer follow-up, most responses that were unconfirmed earlier were later confirmed, Genmab said.
The response rate was 81% among first-line patients with left-sided tumours. For patients whose cancer had spread to the liver, which Genmab called a poor prognostic factor, rates were 76% in the first-line group and 67% in the second-line group. The disease control rate was 95% in first-line and 93% in second-line patients.
The data cover 79 patients treated as of May 15, 2026: 45 in the first-line setting and 34 in the second-line setting.
At the data cutoff, 76% of first-line and 74% of second-line patients remained on treatment. Patients received petosemtamab plus chemotherapy regimens FOLFOX or FOLFIRI in an open-label, single-arm study.
Petosemtamab-related side effects led to discontinuation of the drug in 2 of 42 patients, or 5%, who received it with FOLFOX and in 1 of 37, or 3%, who received it with FOLFIRI.
Genmab reported no side effects leading to death. Infusion-related reactions occurred in 48% of patients on the FOLFOX combination and 43% on FOLFIRI. Grade 3 reactions occurred in 3 of 42 patients, or 7%, and 1 of 37, or 3%, respectively.
Tahamtan Ahmadi, Genmab’s chief medical officer, said the results provide "a compelling rationale" for the company’s ongoing Phase 3 trials. Genmab has Phase 3 trials under way in first- and second-line RAS/BRAF wild-type colorectal cancer.
The results were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress in Madrid.
On Oct. 24, Genmab and biopharmaceutical company Incyte announced a clinical trial collaboration to test petosemtamab with Incyte’s experimental KRAS G12D inhibitor, INCB161734, and standard chemotherapy in first-line patients whose metastatic colorectal cancer carries a KRAS G12D mutation.
Genmab will run the Phase 1/2 study, and Incyte will co-fund it and supply INCB161734. KRAS mutations occur in about 40% of colorectal cancers, with G12D the most common.

Analyst Timothy Moe's conclusion is unambiguous: "The Korean equity market appears deeply undervalued and offers over 60% upside from current levels."
The target reduction, he explains, is a concession to near-term sentiment rather than a shift in the fundamental view.
"[We] incorporate more conservative assumptions about how the market may price underlying fundamentals but still view the market as offering attractive risk/reward at current levels."
After surging more than 300% between April 2025 and June 2026, the KOSPI has since fallen 40%, retracing half of its prior bull run, according to Goldman's analysis. That decline has happened against a backdrop of record corporate profits, making the valuation compression particularly jarring. The 12-month forward P/E has collapsed to 4x, a level Goldman describes as 3 standard deviations below the historical mean.
Goldman attributes roughly half of the 40% drop to a volatility-driven de-rating rather than any deterioration in earnings.
"The 4 s.d. recent spike in volatility coincided with a 2pp increase in the equity risk premium. This equates to a 20% P/B de-rating, which explains half the equity market's 40% decline from its June peak."
The implication is that a normalization of risk sentiment alone could recover a substantial portion of lost ground, independent of any earnings improvement.
The semiconductor memory sector sits at the center of the selloff narrative. Goldman estimates that at current price-to-book levels, the KOSPI's semiconductor cohort is pricing in a 65% decline in 2027 earnings, a scenario Moe calls "overly negative based on the current outlook."
Retail derisking, notably through leveraged ETFs, has amplified the move, and the contagion has spread well beyond the memory names themselves.
Non-memory sectors, which account for roughly half of the KOSPI's index weight, now trade at 7.6x next-twelve-month P/E, or 2.1 standard deviations below their historical mean, alongside a 1.1x price-to-book ratio.
Goldman calculates that implies more than 30% undervaluation relative to a 14.2% return on equity for those businesses.
"Our conclusion is that the market is pricing an overly negative fundamental outlook," the analyst added.
Even the 9,000 target Goldman now uses as its base case leaves room for further upside. At that level, the KOSPI would trade at 6.5x consensus forward P/E and 1.5x price-to-book versus a 23% return on equity, metrics at which Goldman says the market would still be more than 20% undervalued.

One near-term headwind Goldman acknowledges is earnings estimate momentum. title: Anthropic files for IPO, with revenue surging and potential $2 trillion valuation
full_text:
Investing.com -- Anthropic publicly filed for an initial public offering on Monday, seeking to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT, as the artificial intelligence company disclosed explosive revenue growth alongside enormous computing commitments and warnings that losses will continue.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the offering. Anthropic has not yet disclosed its targeted valuation or the number of shares it plans to sell.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the company could provide those details in roughly two weeks, after gauging investor feedback. Anthropic is targeting a public listing in the week of Nov. 16, though the timing could change, according to people familiar with the matter cited by the Journal. The IPO could raise $100 billion or more and value the company at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, the report said.
Anthropic reported revenue of $16.3 billion for the six months ended June 30, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss reached $80.7 billion, compared with a loss of $13 billion in the same period last year, according to the filing. Approximately $72 billion of the latest loss reflected a non-cash accounting charge tied to changes in the value of convertible notes and other financing instruments, Reuters reported, citing the prospectus.
The company warned that it may not achieve or sustain profitability, expects costs to increase over time and anticipates continued losses. It also cautioned that its revenue growth may not be sustainable and that its rate of growth could decrease.
Enterprise demand accelerates
Anthropic’s customer base has expanded rapidly alongside its revenue. The company had more than 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 in revenue, up from 950 a year earlier. As of Sept. 30, more than 1,900 customers generated at least $1 million in revenue on a trailing-12-month basis, while about 250 generated more than $10 million.
Net revenue retention reached approximately 900% as of Sept. 30, according to the filing. The metric measures revenue growth from existing customers, including the effects of expansion, contraction and customer departures. The figure points to a substantial increase in spending among Anthropic’s existing customer base.
Computing commitments and financing needs
The company’s rapid growth comes with enormous infrastructure requirements. Anthropic disclosed $245 billion in future minimum payment obligations, along with additional short-term agreements carrying approximately $21 billion in minimum payments.
The company also disclosed major commitments to infrastructure providers. It expects to spend up to approximately $114.5 billion with Google through 2033 and at least $110 billion with Amazon through 2036. Anthropic separately reported plans to spend up to $120.5 billion on computing involving SpaceXAI and Nvidia. The company has also entered into five-year master equipment leases with Broadcom, with rent payments over the life of those leases totaling approximately $161.2 billion.
These figures cover different agreements and categories of obligations and should not be treated as a single, additive estimate of total infrastructure spending.
Anthropic warned that capital expenditures will increase significantly and that it expects substantial cash requirements over the longer term. Net cash use could rise even if business performance improves, the company cautioned, underscoring the challenge of translating rapid AI adoption into sustainable cash generation.
Anthropic had $112.4 billion in cash and cash equivalents as of June 30 and had raised $141.1 billion in capital by that date, according to the filing.
The company also disclosed a $15 billion revolving credit agreement entered into in September, increasing revolving commitments from $3.3 billion. It raised its minimum liquidity covenant from $500 million to $5 billion and extended the facility’s maturity to September 2031.
Anthropic may issue up to $42 billion in convertible promissory notes to finance rent obligations. Amazon has also agreed to provide up to $20 billion in financing under an April agreement, according to the filing.
Governance, AI risks and public-benefit commitments
Anthropic is incorporated as a public benefit corporation and has created a Long-Term Benefit Trust. Its founders have pledged to donate 80% of their equity to charity, while the filing provides for a special Class T stock for Class T directors.
The company also committed to keeping Claude free of advertising, distinguishing its approach from AI services that may seek to monetize consumer usage through ads.
The filing highlights risks beyond the company’s financial commitments. Anthropic warned of potentially catastrophic, existential risks to humanity from advanced AI, adding that risks could grow as AI systems increasingly automate research and development of AI itself. The prospectus also discusses scenarios in which advanced models could exhibit self-preserving behavior, resist shutdown or manipulate information. These are risks identified by the company, not assertions that such outcomes are routine.
Anthropic plans to invest $325 million in a newly formed entity intended to accelerate AI adoption among midsize companies. It also said it does not expect to pay dividends in the foreseeable future.
The company disclosed that Amazon purchased 19.3 million Series G-2 non-voting shares. Anthropic also repurchased approximately 4.5 million Series B shares from the United States in October 2025.
The IPO would give public-market investors exposure to one of the leading developers of large language models as businesses expand their use of AI. Anthropic’s revenue growth, expanding enterprise relationships and high net revenue retention point to strong demand for its products. But its substantial long-term infrastructure commitments, expectations for rising capital expenditures and warning that losses will continue put cash generation and the economics of AI infrastructure at the center of the investment case.
The potential $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation reported by the Wall Street Journal would put Anthropic among the world’s most highly valued companies. Whether public-market investors will accept that price for a business with extraordinary growth but substantial long-term financial obligations remains a key question as the IPO approaches.

title: Why Goldman Sachs expects Fed to skip October rate hike

Investing.com -- Goldman Sachs expects the Federal Reserve to hold rates at this week’s meeting but deliver a second hike in December, stating in a note Monday that FOMC participants appear to have settled on a compromise of raising rates at every other meeting.

However, he noted that the tightening is only slightly more than is usually associated with one rate hike, and much less than the four hikes the market had priced. As a result, the FOMC is unlikely to view it as excessive or as a replacement for hikes.

“We do not expect a hike in March because we expect the inflation trend to improve as the effects of tariffs, the energy shock, and AI price pressures diminish,” the economist said.
However, Goldman said a March hike is possible if inflation data come in worse than expected.
“The most important risk is that oil futures are above our forecasts, largely reflecting concerns about potential further conflict with Iran,” Mericle said.

title: Analysts forecast Brazil market plunge after Lula turnaround win
full_text:
Oct 26 (Reuters) - Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s election victory over Flavio Bolsonaro looked set to trigger a sharp selloff in its financial markets on Monday.
Brazil’s stock market hit a record high after the first round of the election earlier this month pointed to a Bolsonaro win, boosting investor hopes for a more fiscally disciplined government and a wave of pro-business policies.
MORGAN STANLEY ANALYST NOTE"The first step (in market reaction) would be simply reversing the first-round decline in fiscal risk premia: We estimate this could be a very fast adjustment of ~200bp across the board, towards 14.50% on Jan 29 DIs (interbank rates).
"The markets are likely to price out quickly most, if not all of the ~130bp of easing priced into the front-end of the "Brazilian interbank rate) curve given first round optimism. We would expect USD/BRL to test 5.50"
"If Lula’s new government doesn’t commit to spending cuts in the coming weeks "then we would likely slide closer to the bear
case ... one where asset prices incorporate fiscal dominance risks. "In our view, this would translate into USD/BRL to
6.00, Jan-29 DIs (interbank rates) to 16.50% ... Market pricing would start to include rate hikes and BCB intervention to stabilize BRL would become more likely."
ABERDEEN INVESTMENTS EM DEBT DIRECTOR, VIKTOR SZABÓ
"The concern is not simply who won, but how.
"In the three weeks between the two rounds, the government brought forward a 15% increase in Bolsa Família, the flagship cash-transfer programme.
"It cut federal taxes on petrol to zero and increased subsidies for ethanol and imported diesel. Lula signed into law the forgiveness of federal tax debts owed by micro-entrepreneurs."
"Days before the vote, the government sent Congress a constitutional amendment for free public transport at weekends and on public holidays. Congress also promulgated the end of the six-day working week, one of Lula’s flagship pledges.
"Taken together, they send an unmistakable signal: when votes were at stake, fiscal prudence came second."
RBC BLUEBAY SENIOR EM STRATEGIST, GRAHAM STOCK
"We expect DIs (the local swap market) and the currency to open down, circuit breakers will kick in, so I’m not sure how much trading there will be (during Monday’s session).
"It depends on how Lula and his team react – the market was clearly signalling it preferred (Bolsonaro’s pledges of) fiscal consolidation – so the question is how much Lula will adjust his stance.
"How that is reconciled is key, but we might not get a resolution for months, as he (Lula) will have build a coalition to work with congress ... The lesson will be that policy will have to be tighter than in his third term."
BARCLAYS ANALYST NOTE
"Lula’s victory should trigger disorderly moves in local markets," Barclays analysts said in a note.
"USDBRL could initially go to the 5.50 range ...markets will be looking to the Ministry of Finance pick, along with signals about the policy agenda following the campaign promises that would point to a looser fiscal stance."
They added that Brazilian sovereign bonds could sell off around 300 basis points in the coming days, mirroring moves after the last election in 2022 when Lula announced his cabinet and less constrained spending plans.
Speculation around a contested election was "typically something markets look through, but could be in the headlines if a potential annulment is discussed."
ING STRATEGIST CHRIS TURNER IN LONDON
"Expect Brazilian markets to be hit hard. USD/BRL gapping 5-7% higher at the open to the 5.20/25 area should be no surprise, while the local Bovespa equity index looks set for double-digit losses.
"The moves could turn out to be larger if the external environment deteriorates again and US Treasury yields spike. The fiscal side has always been Brazil’s Achilles heel, and a 7-8% budget deficit and 70% net debt-to-GDP ratio leave Brazil vulnerable in a global bond sell-off.
"Important for local financial markets will be how quickly Bolsonaro accepts the result – or at least allows the constitution to run its course. That is what his father did 44 hours after losing to Lula in 2022, a move that provided some calm to markets."
JPMORGAN ANALYST NOTE
On Equities – "It is important to keep in mind that circuit breakers are likely on Monday: a 10% decline in the Ibov (stock market) leads to a 30 minute market paralysis, a 15% decline triggers an additional 1 hour break, and a 20% decline gives the B3 the discretion to suspend trading for the rest of the day. We expect at least part of that to happen.
"In terms of sectors, the domestic cyclicals should fall hard, while exporters should outperform on the back of currency weakness."
JPMorgan analysts also cut their view on Brazil’s government bonds to "underweight", effectively a recommendation to sell.
"Brazil’s (bond) spread outperformance vs. BB-rated peers and a greater tilt toward Eurobond financing leaves (the) sovereign credit exposed to a meaningful correction unless – and until – market pressure prompts fiscal concessions."
AVIVA INVESTORS SENIOR PORTFOLIO MANAGER, KURT KNOWLSON
"We expect a negative market reaction to Lula’s election victory.
"The announced measures by the Lula administration in the run-up to the second round mean that the starting point for much-needed fiscal consolidation is higher now.
"The reality is that Brazilian real weakness and higher long-end and real rates will again be needed to provide the disciplining mechanism, unless a credible fiscal path can be announced in short order."
CAPITAL ECONOMICS’ ANALYST, WILLIAM JACKSON
"Lula’s surprise win in the second round of Brazil’s presidential election will dash hopes for reforms that would improve the public finances and strengthen growth prospects. A sharp fall in the real and equities and a rise in bond yields, more than reversing the rally since the first-round vote, are likely."

title: Anthropic’s IPO: 7 risks investors should know before buying
full_text:
Investing.com -- Revenue is soaring, but Anthropic’s (NASDAQ:ANT) IPO prospectus warns of risks that go far beyond ordinary tech sector challenges, from enormous computing commitments to AI systems that can behave in unexpected and potentially dangerous ways.
Anthropic, the company behind Claude, is preparing to enter the public markets. Its S-1 registration statement, filed earlier today, reveals a business growing at extraordinary speed and a set of risks investors should not overlook.
Revenue reached $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier. But Anthropic explicitly warns that past growth is no guarantee of future performance. Here are seven key risks highlighted in its prospectus.
1. Winning the AI race requires staggering resources
Anthropic needs vast amounts of computing power to train and run its models. If it cannot secure enough capacity, competitors could overtake it. But committing to too much capacity could leave the company paying for expensive, underused infrastructure.
The timing makes this especially challenging: computing agreements can lock Anthropic into substantial payments even if customer demand slows. Access to chips, electricity and data centers could also become constrained.
The risk: Anthropic could face rising costs and inflexible commitments just as its growth begins to slow.
2. AI could behave in ways the company cannot control
Perhaps the most striking disclosures concern AI safety.
Anthropic warns that its models could act unexpectedly, circumvent safeguards, cause harm or behave in ways that diverge from human intentions. During cybersecurity evaluations, four models gained unauthorized access to real third-party computer systems after a testing configuration error left internet access enabled. In one incident, a model obtained administrator access and accessed personal information.
Anthropic said it found no evidence that the models were deliberately evading oversight. Nevertheless, the company acknowledges that increasingly autonomous AI could create more serious risks, including potentially catastrophic incidents. It also warns that insurance might not cover the full costs of a major disaster.
The risk: A serious incident could damage customer trust, trigger lawsuits and regulatory action, and threaten the business itself.
3. Safety measures could slow product development
Anthropic faces a difficult balancing act: develop more capable models quickly enough to compete, while ensuring they are safe to deploy.
The company disclosed that it delayed pre-training a new flagship model for more than a month to strengthen protections against theft of model weights and intellectual property.
Future safety reviews could cause further delays. Conversely, deploying models before safeguards are adequate could create security, reputational and legal problems.
The risk: Anthropic could lose ground by moving too slowly — or face serious consequences by moving too quickly.
4. Revenue growth may not translate into lasting profits
Anthropic warns that its historical growth rates are not sustainable assumptions for the future. Customers may reduce spending, competitors may offer cheaper alternatives, and businesses may build their own AI systems.
There is another complication: increasingly autonomous AI agents can consume more computing resources than conventional AI services. If Anthropic cannot charge enough to cover those costs, expanding usage could put pressure on margins.
The risk: Even strong demand may not produce sustainable profitability if delivering AI remains extraordinarily expensive.
5. Competition and customer concentration threaten growth
Anthropic faces intense competition in a rapidly changing market. A competitor that develops superior models or offers comparable capabilities at lower prices could attract customers and weaken Anthropic’s position.
The business also relies on a limited number of large customers and distribution channels. Its five largest customers accounted for approximately 25% of revenue during the first nine months of 2026. Major cloud partners also have their own AI businesses, creating potential conflicts of interest.
The risk: Losing key customers, partners or its technological edge could have a disproportionate impact.
6. Lawsuits and regulation could increase costs
Questions surrounding AI training data, copyright, privacy and intellectual property remain legally contentious. Adverse court decisions could force Anthropic to pay damages, obtain additional licenses or modify its models.
Regulators could also impose stricter requirements on AI safety, transparency, data handling and deployment. International trade restrictions and geopolitical tensions could further limit access to customers, technology or markets.
The risk: Legal and regulatory changes could increase costs, restrict products or undermine Anthropic’s competitive position.
7. Investors may have limited control
Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, with a stated mission of developing advanced AI responsibly for humanity’s long-term benefit. That mission may guide decisions that do not maximize short-term profits.
Its proposed governance structure reinforces that distinction. The founders’ entity is set to hold a single Class F share carrying 50.1% of general voting power, while the Long-Term Benefit Trust has significant influence over board composition.
The risk: Ordinary shareholders may have limited influence over strategic decisions, including how the company balances safety, growth and financial returns.
The bottom line
Anthropic’s prospectus presents a company with enormous potential — but also significant uncertainty. Its biggest challenges include securing computing capacity, managing AI safety, converting demand into sustainable profits and maintaining its competitive advantage.
And even if Anthropic succeeds, investors can still lose money by paying too high a price.
Before buying shares, investors should examine the final IPO valuation (estimated at $2 trillion), the company’s path to profitability, its long-term infrastructure commitments, and the implications of its governance structure.
The question is not just whether AI will transform the economy. It is whether Anthropic can turn that transformation into lasting shareholder value at a price that adequately compensates investors for the risks.

title: Brazil finance minister signals more ambitious primary surplus for next year
full_text:
BRASILIA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Brazil’s Finance Minister, Dario Durigan, said in an interview with local news service Broadcast on Monday that the government will pursue a higher effective primary surplus next year, although he did not specify a figure.
Following a sweeping selloff across Brazilian markets triggered by fiscal concerns over the reelection of leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Durigan also said the government plans to send legislation to Congress this year requiring policymakers to formally target the midpoint of the primary balance goal.
The minister said the Treasury had intervened in the government bond market on Monday by canceling scheduled debt auctions and conducting extraordinary buyback operations to "ensure rationality" in trading after a sharp jump in long-term interest rate futures triggered by the election.
"But in the short, medium and long term, we will return to discussing fiscal stability, formally pursue the midpoint of the target and raise our surplus projection for next year," Broadcast quoted Durigan as saying.
Brazil’s fiscal target for next year calls for a primary surplus, excluding interest payments, of 0.5% of GDP, with a tolerance band of 0.25 percentage point on either side.
Under the fiscal framework, however, the government can exclude certain expenditures when assessing compliance, most notably part of its stock of court-ordered debt payments.
In August, the government projected an effective primary surplus of 0.1% of GDP for next year. If achieved, it would be Brazil’s first fiscal surplus since 2022.
Most investors and economists, however, view that pace of fiscal consolidation as too slow given the rapid growth of mandatory spending, pushing investors to demand ever-higher premiums to hold Brazilian debt.
Brazil’s gross public debt, the government’s main solvency indicator, is up more than 10 percentage points during Lula’s current term to 82.9% of GDP.

title: Trump administration loses push to block California votes from alleged noncitizens
full_text:
By Luc Cohen and Jan Wolfe
Oct 26 (Reuters) - A US appeals court on Monday ruled against President Donald Trump’s administration in a major voting dispute ahead of the midterm elections, denying a request to block California from counting mail ballots from people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government alleges are likely noncitizens.
The 2-1 decision by the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals marked the latest setback in Trump’s efforts to assert a greater federal role in overseeing elections in the run-up to the November 3 midterms in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress.
The majority decision said the Justice Department had failed to give a lower court judge an adequate opportunity to consider the case, and therefore it would be premature for the appeals court to weigh in. The lower court judge has scheduled a hearing on Tuesday in the case.
Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, one of the two judges in the majority, wrote in a concurring opinion that the federal government "asks the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain, upending the state’s policies in this regard and inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike."
The lawsuit was an escalation in the Trump administration’s pressure on state election officials over alleged noncitizen voting and a rare intervention by the Justice Department in the voting process weeks before an election.
The California lawsuit was the first time the Trump administration sought to prevent a state from counting votes, though it did not indicate how many of the 20,000 people on its list had actually submitted a mail ballot.
Justice Department officials said on October 19 that the 20,000 people included 28 who had been criminally charged with illegally voting.
California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives — 52 — than any other state. Democrats are seeking to regain control of the House from Trump’s fellow Republicans in the midterms.
Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its "sanctuary state" policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
Trump has long asserted that California’s immigration policies have facilitated voter fraud.
All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including noncitizen voting, is exceedingly rare. A Reuters investigation published in July found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud.
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on October 15 in federal court in Los Angeles. The lawsuit asked a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration’s list from the rest of the ballots, and not to count them until it had verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens.
The Justice Department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case.
California says the state’s safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust, and asserted in a court filing that the Justice Department’s assertions relied on "suspect data."
"At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt," lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in an October 20 court filing. "At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election."
Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the Trump administration’s methods for scrutinizing state voter lists to identify noncitizens risk wrongly flagging naturalized US citizens for removal from the rolls.
The Justice Department has told election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their rolls or cast ballots. It has sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for refusing to provide complete voter rolls including voters’ sensitive personal data, but has lost 26 of those cases so far without winning one.
"Today’s ruling is a positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump’s disgusting attacks on the Constitution and our country’s democracy," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat.

title: JetBlue seeks to reassure investors as losses deepen
full_text:
By Doyinsola Oladipo and Nandan Mandayam
Oct 26 (Reuters) - JetBlue Airways sought to reassure investors about its financial health on Monday despite posting a bigger-than-expected quarterly loss, as a sharp selloff in its bonds and mounting restructuring concerns cast a shadow over the airline’s turnaround.
JetBlue’s shares jumped 11% in volatile trading after the bell, recovering some losses after they closed down nearly 10% following a report that the airline’s creditors were working with restructuring advisers amid a bond selloff.
Even as management insists its liquidity is sufficient to satisfy the company’s needs for at least the next 12 months, shares have fallen 48% year to date, while short interest in the stock is now at 26%.
JetBlue’s TrueBlue senior secured note, a bond backed by the airline’s loyalty program, came under heavy selling pressure this month, with the price halving to about $47 and yields surging to distressed levels above 30%.
The carrier raised its full-year forecast for seat revenue growth to 13.5% to 14.5%, from its earlier range of 10% to 12.5%. It attributed the improved outlook to higher fares and its expansion in Fort Lauderdale, but acknowledged ongoing challenges from surging fuel costs and operating losses.
JetBlue said it was able to recover 87% of its fuel costs in the third quarter as fares rose across the industry with no meaningful decline in passenger volume.
US airlines have relied on fare hikes, ancillary fees and capacity controls to boost revenue, as they grapple with volatile fuel prices that make it harder to forecast costs and earnings.
JetBlue said it paid about $3.91 per gallon of fuel in the July-September quarter, up 57% from a year ago, and slightly below the $3.96-a-gallon rate it had forecast last month. Unit revenue, a measure of pricing power, rose just 18.4%, lagging the spike in fuel costs.
The airline posted an adjusted loss of 60 cents per share for the three months to September 30, compared with a 40-cent loss in the year-ago period. Analysts expected a loss of 55 cents per share, according to data compiled by LSEG.
CASH WOES
JetBlue ended the third quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity, including a $600 million undrawn credit facility, and about $7 billion in unencumbered assets — $2.8 billion of which are aircraft and engines, following updated appraisals.
However, cash and cash equivalents fell to $1.26 billion from $1.66 billion at mid-year, and total cash and investments have dropped by about $850 million, or a third, since December.
Total debt declined to $8.39 billion from $8.5 billion in the prior quarter, but the company continues to burn cash at an accelerating pace.
JetBlue used $273 million more cash than it generated from operations in the first nine months of 2026 — nearly twice the $143 million cash burn in the same period last year. This shrinking cushion leaves the airline with less room to maneuver as it faces ongoing losses and upcoming debt maturities, increasing pressure to raise additional funds if the trend continues.
Still, the airline reiterated its target of at least $1 in earnings per share and positive free cash flow in 2028.
It expects operating margin to further improve in the fourth quarter, even with the price of fuel being 85% higher year over year.

title: Ex-FBI chief Comey faces third prosecution attempt by Trump Justice Department
full_text:
WASHINGTON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department is attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey for a third time, the latest case accusing him of sharing sensitive national security information in 2016, according to court documents made public on Monday.
The case was revealed in a court document known as a "criminal information" that the Justice Department said it filed to stop the 10-year statute of limitations on the offense from expiring earlier this month.
The document filed in Washington federal court charges Comey with transmitting and conspiring to transmit national defense information. It alleges he shared classified information with a reporter from the New York Times in October 2016.
Comey said in a video on Instagram that "they’re back again" and referenced the Justice Department, but did not provide further details. "I’m still innocent," he added. Comey’s lawyers have already asked a judge to dismiss the case, arguing it is legally improper.
The new case adds to the legal fights facing Comey, whom the Justice Department has already charged twice, accusing him of lying to Congress about media leaks and threatening President Donald Trump in a social media post. A judge dismissed the false statements case, while the threats case remains pending.
Comey’s lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement that the document "purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit." The criminal information was filed on October 5, but was unsealed on Monday at the request of Comey’s lawyers.
A Justice Department spokesperson described the maneuver to halt the statute of limitations as a "widely recognized practice in federal court."
"This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further," the spokesperson said in a statement.

title: South Korea’s economy grows faster than expected in third quarter
full_text:
SEOUL, Oct 27 (Reuters) - South Korea’s economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter on booming chip exports, advance central bank estimates showed on Tuesday.
Gross domestic product expanded 1.0% in the July-September quarter from the preceding three months, when it grew 0.6%. It was stronger than a median 0.7% increase tipped in a Reuters poll of economists.
Amid the global boom in AI investment, South Korea’s exports topped $800 billion in January to September, higher than last year’s full-year record, and are on track to exceed $1 trillion this year, which will make South Korea the fourth country to reach the milestone, after the US, China and Germany.
The Bank of Korea kept interest rates unchanged last week, after back-to-back hikes in July and September, but maintained a hawkish stance by upgrading its economic growth forecasts and remaining upbeat about the country’s export momentum.
In the third quarter, exports rose 2.3% on demand for semiconductors, machinery and electric equipment, while imports grew 2.4%.
Facilities investment jumped 4.1%, led by machinery such as semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Private consumption fell 0.2%, the first decline in nearly four years.
On a year-on-year basis, GDP grew 3.4%, after rising 3.7% in the quarter before, according to the Bank of Korea, also stronger than economists’ expectations for a 3.0% increase.

title: Exclusive-US, Canada working on deal to ease steel, auto tariffs, sources say
full_text:
By Promit Mukherjee and David Shepardson
OTTAWA/WASHINGTON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - The United States and Canada are working on a deal to ease US tariffs on Canadian steel and autos, two US and four Canadian sources said, as the two governments try to repair relations that soured after trade talks broke down in August.
The talks focus on tariffs imposed under Section 232 of US trade law, including up to 50% tariff on Canadian steel and a 25% tariff on autos, with negotiators discussing potential relief from those duties.
Just 32% of Americans approve of US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in next week’s midterm elections. Tariffs on Canadian imports have become a political liability for Trump, with Republican candidates in border states calling for an end to the trade war with Canada.
One Canadian source briefed on the negotiations said a deal on steel and auto tariffs was possible before the November 3 elections, while US sources said the Trump administration wanted Canada to make further concessions. The sources spoke on condition of anonymity because the talks are private.
The Section 232 tariffs are administered by the Commerce Department, putting Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick rather than the US Trade Representative’s office at the center of the negotiations, sources on both sides of the border said.
Lutnick and Canada’s Dominic LeBlanc, the minister responsible for Canada-US trade, have been in regular contact recently, one of the sources said.
"Canada remains in constructive dialogue with our U.S. counterparts on a range of priorities," a spokesperson for LeBlanc, said in a statement. "We stand ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada’s interests.”
The US Trade Representative’s Office and Canada have also been in contact in recent days regarding the overall architecture of any deal and all other trade issues, a USTR official said.
The White House and the Commerce Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
OTTAWA SEES PROGRESS
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said there had been "a slight intensification" in talks with the United States, adding that Ottawa had not changed its stance.
"To the extent any progress has been made, it’s because the US is coming closer to our position," he told reporters, but did not give details.
A Canadian industry source said a deal could come quickly, but not necessarily a broad one. "If it happens, it’ll happen fast. But my sense is it’ll be a narrowed deal, if it even happens,” the source said.
Another Canadian source said they have believed for some time that a deal on Section 232 tariffs is likely before the midterms. Any agreement would be driven by Trump and Carney, the source said, adding that both leaders had said a mutually beneficial deal is possible.
Carney has said he wants a good deal for Canada.
US and Canadian trade talks collapsed in August over issues such as whether to cut duties on medium- and heavy-duty vehicles that are critical for Canadian factories. US automakers had hoped the trade talks would deliver relief from Washington’s original 25% tariffs that have raised the cost of shipping vehicles and parts across the border.
Trump has previously announced that he would raise the tariffs on steel and auto imports from Canada to 50% from January 1, 2027. At a political rally on Sunday, Trump predicted the trade dispute would be resolved "soon," without providing specifics.
Trump signed an order on Friday to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a move that could benefit businesses in Maine.

title: Analysis-China’s lab-grown diamond makers target AI, chip sectors for next wave of growth
full_text:
By Amy Lv and Casey Hall
ZHENGZHOU, China Oct 27 (Reuters) - Around 70% of the 2 million carats of lab-grown diamonds produced annually at Feng Canjun’s factory currently go into jewellery.
But the entrepreneur is betting that the future of China’s synthetic diamond industry lies in supplying advanced materials for semiconductors, AI servers and other high-tech applications.
"I am looking to raise the share of my products used in functional materials to more than 50% by 2030 while reducing the share going to the jewellery sector to a maximum of 30%," Feng said.
China’s lab-grown diamond producers, which account for around half of the world’s supply, are looking beyond gemstones as competition intensifies and prices come under pressure.
The shift could give the industry greater strategic significance in the US-China technology rivalry. If synthetic diamonds become more widely used in semiconductors and thermal management in AI infrastructure, China’s production dominance could emerge as another supply-chain vulnerability for the US.
"The transition is now the defining structural story in the diamond industry and one with direct implications for global technology supply chains," said Manan Goenka, engagement manager at Ken Research, a consultancy.
Companies and analysts say demand from sectors including chips, thermal management and quantum technology could become the industry’s next major growth engine, with synthetic diamonds prized for properties that can improve the performance of advanced electronics and computing systems.
The move comes as AI drives a surge in demand for data centre capacity. The International Energy Agency said in a 2025 report that data centre electricity consumption is projected to more than double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, roughly equivalent to Japan’s annual power consumption, with AI being the main driver.
THE AI OPPORTUNITY
Thermal management is viewed by analysts as a nearer-term opportunity, while the use of diamonds as a semiconductor material is further away from widespread commercial adoption. Chip applications also require much higher purity and tighter manufacturing standards than diamonds used in cutting and drilling tools.
But interest from some of the world’s biggest technology companies points to the potential for chip applications to become a new source of demand as AI computing generates increasing amounts of heat.
Chinese media have reported that Huawei and TSMC are exploring synthetic diamonds for chip cooling, while Lenovo has launched a consumer laptop in China that it says uses a diamond-copper cooling material.
In June, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said he personally invested in Diamond Foundry, a lab-grown diamond maker developing chip-grade diamond wafers.
Huawei, Lenovo and Intel did not respond to requests for comment. TSMC declined to comment.
Some Chinese producers are beginning to invest in anticipation of demand. Henan Liliang Diamond plans to redirect 1 billion yuan ($149.18 million) in funds originally raised to expand gem-grade diamond production to a new functional-diamond project, according to a June filing.
In April, diamond-copper cooling modules developed by Chinese researchers improved heat transfer from chip modules by 80% and raised chip performance by 10%, according to the Ningbo Institute of Materials Technology & Engineering.
Wider adoption could reshape the market for thermal-management materials that are used to stop chips from overheating. Germany’s Henkel, US chemical firm Dow and Japan’s Shin-Etsu Chemical sell products used to dissipate heat from chips. Diamond heat spreaders could compete with some existing materials if adopted widely in AI chips and data centres.
Henkel, Dow and Shin-Etsu did not respond to requests for comment.
Related diamond-enabled products are also being explored outside China. In June, De Beers’ synthetic-diamond and advanced-materials business Element Six and Japan’s Orbray said they had produced 3-inch single-crystal diamond wafers and were preparing 2-inch wafers for production in Oregon.
The Spanish government is investing €753 million ($868 million) in a Diamond Foundry plant in Trujillo that will make synthetic diamond wafers. If completed, it would be Europe’s first large-scale producer of diamond substrates, a material for semiconductor manufacturing.
In early October, Frore Systems, a US thermal-management company, unveiled LiquidJet Diamond, a multi-stage coldplate with an integrated diamond spreader.
"The scope and potential in the technology and industrial sectors could be significantly above the retail diamond jewellery business, which itself is approximately $100 billion a year," said independent diamond consultant Robert Bouquet.
DIAMOND MACHINE
Feng’s Jiaruifu factory is one of hundreds of lab-grown producers clustered in the central province of Henan, which accounts for 80% of China’s synthetic diamond output.
Lab-grown diamonds are made in machines that replicate the high-temperature, high-pressure conditions under which natural diamonds form. They are physically identical to mined diamonds.
One machine in Feng’s factory can produce 120 carats of rough diamonds in six days, shortening a process that takes billions of years naturally.
Feng has 550 such machines, each costing about 3 million yuan and weighing more than 100 tons. They have enabled him to increase annual output tenfold since launching the business in 2019, to 2 million carats in 2025, equivalent to about 9% of De Beers’ production last year.
Beijing has already moved to incorporate the technology into its export control regime, placing related machinery and key components under restrictions in 2024. It added more synthetic diamond products to its list in 2025, though implementation was postponed for a year under a US-China deal reached last October.
"The broader implication is that synthetic diamonds could increasingly become part of the strategic trade-policy conversation surrounding semiconductors, rare earths and advanced manufacturing," said Goenka.
China’s rapid expansion of lab-grown diamond production has helped drive down prices, increasing pressure on producers to find higher-value applications.
Gross profit margins are 30% to 40% for gem-grade diamonds compared with about 50% for industrial diamonds, according to Feng. Rather than increasing output further, he plans to shift more production towards higher-value industrial uses.
While the commercial potential of synthetic diamonds in advanced industrial applications remains uncertain and risks contributing to another bout of Chinese industrial overcapacity, producers remain optimistic.
"It will be a billion- or even trillion-yuan market, and we are strategically expanding into next-generation applications to replace traditional ones," Feng said.
($1 = 6.6997 Chinese yuan)
